messages.subject: Re: Regarding assembly support
messages.body_plain:
Hi Shalu,
You have calculated the promoter boundaries incorrectly. Please copy paste the coordinates you calculated to UCSC browser ( mm9) and see if it makes sense ( to me. it doesn't)
http://genome-euro.ucsc.edu/cgi-bin/hgTracks?db=mm9&position=chr1%3A4280825-4281926&hgsid=197570539_alZvCMl4swU5GIhGINbW0f3BiOvC

On top of that, when you are trying to summarize CpGs to promoters, you are taking some sort of average. numCs and numTs columns in the input files should be integers, yours are floats. In addition, you are losing the boundary information by trying to summarize information yourself and reading the file that way. When methylKit reads your files, it treats them as single CpGs.

The easiest thing would be to read-in basepair resolution CpGs and use regionCounts() to do the summary. If you want to make the summary yourself, this is not the correct way to do it.

Best,
Altuna

"3256" "chr13.119601308" "chr13" 119601308 119601308 "+" 5.60865078296767e-06 0.00563332884641272 92.8571428571429

Can anyone tell me if this is an error on my end, have i called the input columns to methylKit wrong or is this perhaps an error in the methylKit code?

Claire

I don't know if UCSC maps one-to-one with ensemble? Same number of lines doesn't not prove mapping is one-to-one. You also have repeating coordinates in your file, I don't think your file contains the same information as the methylKit promoter files. In methylKit file, there is one promoter per unique TSS. There is an argument you can change in read.transcript.features() so that you get one promoter for each transcript, but in that case you will have redundant locations, transcript isoforms having the same TSS will have the same promoter coordinates. see the help page for that function.

Since the last e-mail you are making the same mistake when calculating the promoter coordinates. You can easily verify what you are doing is correct by pasting your coordinates to UCSC browser (as many as you can). If you do that, you will see some of your promoter coordinates doesn't make sense.

here is a coordinate from your file: chr1 4280825 4281925
What you call promoter in that location is the 3' end of the gene, and that is not the promoter but a region around transcription end. And, I think that explains most of the discrepancy.

Here is the UCSC url:
http://genome-euro.ucsc.edu/cgi-bin/hgTracks?db=mm9&position=chr1%3A4280826-4281925&hgsid=197592283_4LZ6nD6R3JhEWLCPr68io8aQYgCm

for the chrM, promoter start coordinate is minus because probably the TSS is close to the start of the chromosome. It shouldn't cause a problem when summarizing the methylation values, you just have to correct for it later on.

Best,
Altuna

messages.subject: methylKit vs. Seqmonk
messages.body_plain:
I’ve been working with a mRRBS dataset and have a bit of time using both methylKit and Seqmonk. I’ve used Bismark to align my bisulfite sequence reads, sorted the outputted SAM files by genomic location and then loaded the data into R using the read.bismark function in methylKit and looking only at the CpG context.

Using the same SAM files, I used Bismark’s methylation extractor to generate the CpG context OT and OB methylation calls, and then loaded those files into Seqmonk.

When I randomly look at the methylRaw values can compare the locations of methylated or unmethylated cytosines and compare them with data loaded into Seqmonk, I’m finding that there are methylRaw values have data for locations that do not correspond with the data loaded into Seqmonk.

Has anyone else experienced this and/or have a reason why methylKit and Seqmonk don’t have the same results?

Thanks,
Ed

Single differentially methylated CpG can indicate something biologically relevant if it overlaps with TFBS site. There are examples that CpG methylation is associated with bound/unbound state of a transcription factor. Some think that TF binding drives de-methylation for some TFs. But probably you will see other CpGs demethylating around such a site if they are close by. These are some what speculative points, you have to see the literature and make up your mind.

Best,
Altuna

messages.body_plain:
Thinking about this, if you accept this naive approach you may be able to do this in an easy way.

Assume conversion rate for a sample is the probability of a converted C is really a C. Then, you can multiply the conversion rate per sample with number of Cs (numCs) and (round it to the nearest integer) to get an expected number of correctly converted Cs.

This can be done using reconstruct() function, where you need to get first a percent methylation matrix (there is a function for that), correct it by multiplying it with the sample conversion rates (each column is a sample), then use reconstruct to get the corrected counts.

best,
altuna
